title: Buttons: The Noisy Truth About a Simple Switch
description: Component lesson. The simplest sensor on the whole chassis hides a surprisingly messy secret at the exact moment you press it.

content.value: A push button is about as simple as a sensor gets: two metal contacts, pressed together or not. It's really the same idea as Module 3's switch, wired so the controller can read its state on a GPIO pin instead of switching motor power directly.

Here's the part that surprises most beginners: those two metal contacts don't touch cleanly. At the microscopic level, they physically bounce against each other several times in the first few milliseconds of a press before finally settling — and a controller reading fast enough sees every single one of those bounces as a separate press.

content.title: 🔘 Watch the raw signal
content.hint: Press the button, then drag the debounce window up until the readout says 'fully hidden'.

content.value: The fix is simple once you know the problem exists: after the first change is detected, wait a short window — 10 to 30 milliseconds is typical — and ignore any further changes during that time. By the time the window ends, the bounce has always settled, and the level you read then is trustworthy.
Debouncing isn't unique to buttons — any mechanical contact (a limit switch, a relay) bounces the same way. The fix is identical everywhere: wait it out before trusting the reading.

Key takeaway: a button's contacts physically bounce for a few milliseconds when pressed, which a fast controller would otherwise count as several presses. Debouncing waits out that bounce window before trusting the signal.

quiz.question: Why does a single button press sometimes look like several presses to a fast controller?
options: The metal contacts physically bounce against each other for a few milliseconds before settling
GPIO pins always report presses twice
quiz.explain: That bounce is a real mechanical effect, present in every physical switch — not a fault in any particular button.

quiz.question: What does debouncing actually do?
options: Physically stops the contacts from bouncing
Ignores signal changes for a short window after the first one, then trusts the settled reading
Makes the button press instantly with zero delay
quiz.explain: It's a software wait, not a mechanical fix — give the bounce time to finish, then read the level once it has settled.

quiz.question: Would a limit switch on a robot arm need debouncing too?
options: Yes — any mechanical contact bounces the same way, so the same fix applies
quiz.explain: Bounce comes from physical metal contacts touching, which is common to any mechanical switch, not just buttons.
